question: Can known links between intervention units and outcome units guide treatment probabilities to improve a conservative variance bound while retaining independent assignment and the same expected treatment total? The target is the average outcome contrast between treating every intervention in each outcome's neighborhood and treating none. A common probability ignores differences in neighborhood overlap, while directly optimizing variance requires unknown potential outcomes.
result: The target is τ_n = μ_1 − μ_0, estimated by the Hájek difference of separately normalized inverse-exposure-weighted outcome means. Define V_env(G_n,p) = (4/n)Σ_{i,j}[r_ij¹(G_n,p) + r_ij⁰(G_n,p) + 2r_ij¹⁰(G_n)]. For independent Bernoulli assignment, interior probabilities, and |Y_i¹|, |Y_i⁰| ≤ 1, the linearization variance scale satisfies σ²_{G_n,p}(Y) ≤ V_env(G_n,p). With 0 < ε < 1/2 and m_nε ≤ B_n ≤ m_n(1−ε), minimizing this convex envelope subject to ε ≤ p_k ≤ 1−ε and Σ_k p_k = B_n has a global solution p_n*. Along growing populations, local interference, bounded target outcomes, uniformly bounded neighborhoods and overlap, probability floors bounded away from zero, and liminf σ²_{G_n,p_n*}(Y) > 0 yield √n(τ̂_H(p_n*)−τ_n)/√σ²_{G_n,p_n*}(Y) ⇒ N(0,1). Consequently, τ̂_H(p_n*) ± z_{1−α/2}√(V_env(G_n,p_n*)/n) has asymptotic coverage at least 1−α. Optimization improves the envelope relative to a feasible homogeneous design; it does not guarantee improvement in actual variance.
mechanism: 1. For each outcome, calculate its all-treated and all-control exposure probabilities: π_i¹ = ∏_{k∈N_i}p_k and π_i⁰ = ∏_{k∈N_i}(1−p_k). Weight observed target exposures by their inverse probabilities, normalize each weighted outcome sum by its weighted exposure count, and subtract the two means. 2. Linearize this difference of ratios using η_i = (T_i/π_i¹−1)(Y_i¹−μ_1) − (C_i/π_i⁰−1)(Y_i⁰−μ_0). Its variance scale is σ² = n Var(n⁻¹Σ_iη_i). 3. For each ordered outcome pair, identify shared interventions S_ij. Their covariance loads are r_ij¹ = ∏_{k∈S_ij}p_k⁻¹−1, r_ij⁰ = ∏_{k∈S_ij}(1−p_k)⁻¹−1, and r_ij¹⁰ = 1{S_ij is nonempty}. These multiply unknown products of centered target outcomes. 4. Bound each such product in absolute value by four, producing the graph-only envelope. 5. Minimize that envelope before randomization under the budget and probability bounds. Interior optimal probabilities have equal marginal envelope scores; unequal scores permit a reducing, budget-preserving transfer. 6. Randomize independently using the chosen probabilities, calculate the Hájek estimate, and use the envelope to set the confidence-interval width.
why_true: Independent assignments make contributions from disjoint intervention neighborhoods independent. In normalized joint-exposure probabilities, nonshared assignment factors cancel, leaving covariance loads determined by shared interventions. Bounded outcomes replace the unknown outcome products with uniform bounds, making allocation possible without observing potential outcomes. Bounded neighborhood sizes and uniform positivity bound the weights and contributions; bounded overlap limits their dependence. Nondegenerate variance supplies the scale needed for a central limit theorem. The ratio-estimator remainder vanishes at the √n scale, transferring normality to the Hájek estimator. Using an upper bound on its asymptotic variance then gives coverage at least nominal.
example: When every outcome has one intervention neighbor, intervention k serves s_k outcomes and contributes s_k² ordered pairs. The envelope becomes (4/n)Σ_k s_k²[p_k⁻¹+(1−p_k)⁻¹]. At homogeneous probability ρ, the derivative of one quarter of the envelope is g_k = n⁻¹s_k²[(1−ρ)⁻²−ρ⁻²]. With unequal incidences, interior ρ, and ρ ≠ 1/2, the scores differ, so transferring probability from a higher-score intervention to a lower-score intervention strictly reduces the envelope. This favors higher-incidence interventions when ρ < 1/2 and lower-incidence interventions when ρ > 1/2.
